title: Satyavati
hook: Bhishma carries off three princesses for Satyavati's boy king, and the eldest tells the court her heart is already given

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati lost her husband and her proud elder son, and a boy, Vichitravirya, was left on the throne — a boy king, a queen mother, a vow. Which small argument did you let go? Day seven hundred nineteen.

Word reaches Hastinapura: the king of Kashi has three daughters, and they'll choose their husbands at a swayamvara, a self-choice, with kings gathered from everywhere. Vichitravirya has grown into a young man, and Bhishma has decided he should marry. So, with Satyavati's leave, Bhishma rides out alone in a single chariot to the city of Varanasi. He doesn't go there to be chosen. He goes there to take, and the whole court will watch him do it.
screen: `THREE PRINCESSES OF KASHI.` → `A SELF-CHOICE.` → `BHISHMA RIDES ALONE.`

segments.voice: Bhishma arrives, and the kings there laugh at the old man come courting. He answers by lifting the three princesses onto his chariot. Then, before them all, he names the ways a bride may be won, and says that a bride carried off by force is held in high regard by the wise. The kings take up their weapons, and he fights them, and defeats them, one after another, including the king of Saubha, named Shalva. Then he brings the three sisters home to Satyavati, as if they were his own daughters, the text says. It's a hard scene to hear today, and the text tells it without apology. Then the story turns. As the wedding is prepared, the eldest sister, Amba, speaks. She tells Bhishma that in her heart she had already chosen Shalva, and that he had chosen her. You know dharma, she says. Do what's right. And Bhishma, the man who just won her by force, stops. He consults the learned men of the court, and he lets her go to Shalva. Her story doesn't end there; the Mahabharata comes back to Amba much later, and we'll meet her again. The younger two, Ambika and Ambalika, marry Vichitravirya. And for a while, the text says, the young king is devoted to them and they to him. Then he falls ill with a wasting sickness, and despite his friends and his physicians, he dies, still young, with no son. And Satyavati, who has now outlived a husband and two sons, is left with a palace, two young widows, and a stepson who swore he'd never be king.
screen: `A SELF-CHOICE AT VARANASI.` · `CARRIED OFF BY FORCE.` · `AMBA SPEAKS.` · `A YOUNG KING DIES WITHOUT A SON.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the shoulders soften. In a room full of men who'd already decided her life, Amba said what was true for her. Bring to mind one thing you've left unsaid, because the decision seemed made already, or the room seemed too full. You don't have to say it now. Just let yourself know it clearly. Breathe in, and let the words form. Breathe out, and let them rest, ready. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. A queen mother whose house gains two brides, lets one go, and loses its young king.
Your line: she had already chosen. Today, when a decision about you seems already made, say one true thing about it anyway. Day seven hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In the epics a swayamvara is a gathering where a princess chooses her husband from the suitors; Hindu weddings today come about in other ways, and the word is still known through these stories.

match.prompt: the three sisters — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you're Amba. you've been carried to a strange court and the wedding is being prepared. what do you do?
options: tell Bhishma your heart is given to Shalva.
slip away from the palace at night.
fork.reveal: she speaks, and Bhishma, after consulting the learned men, lets her go. the poem returns to her much later.

original.note: Sanskrit svayamvara: the self-choice, where a princess picks her husband from gathered suitors.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old warrior's daring raid.
what it means: three women's lives decided for them, and the one who speaks up.
what a scholar hears: Amba's story is left open here, and the poem picks it up again much later.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Bhishma wins the daughters of the king of Kashi; Amba released; Vichitravirya's marriage and death)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Bhishma goes with Satyavati's permission in a single chariot to Varanasi; the kings mock him; his speech on the forms of marriage and the regard for a bride taken by force; the defeat of Shalva (spelled Salwa in Ganguli), king of Saubha; Amba's appeal to dharma; the consultation with Brahmanas; Vichitravirya's devotion and death of a wasting disease (phthisis in Ganguli).
The number of years of Vichitravirya's marriage is left out under the claims rule.
Amba's later story (Udyoga Parva) is only foreshadowed, not told.
Abduction is described plainly and called hard to hear today; a Keeper may wish to adjust that framing.
howItsDone makes a general statement about modern weddings; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
Editor pass: review matches 718's revised carry; 'the part that matters most' (narrator ranking) cut; 'usually'/'mostly' generalizations in howItsDone removed.
